strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely bottleneck in Lean autoformalization: retrieving relevant formal-library dependencies from informal mathematical statements.

The generation-plus-verification framing is sensible, and using a suffix-array check to validate generated dependency names is a practical engineering idea for filtering hallucinated identifiers at scale.

The empirical results show large gains for DDR over the selected retrieval baselines on dependency precision/recall, and consistent downstream gains for RA+DDR over RA and RA+R@k on BEq across most difficulty splits.
The paper connects the retrieval task to downstream autoformalization rather than evaluating retrieval in isolation, which strengthens the relevance of the contribution.
The authors acknowledge a real limitation of DDR: generated abbreviated names do not recover full library metadata and are not directly compatible with richer retrieval-augmented pipelines.
weaknesses: The experimental design leaves substantial uncertainty about soundness. DDR is a fine-tuned 32B generative model, while the main retrieval baselines are fixed top-k methods from prior work; the comparison does not isolate whether gains come from the DDR paradigm, model capacity, supervised fine-tuning, or the verification step.

The dependency labels appear to be automatically extracted from formal code via string/suffix matching, but the paper does not adequately validate that these labels correspond to true semantic dependencies. This can introduce false positives, miss implicit dependencies, and create an evaluation metric aligned with the proposed method rather than the underlying task.

The retrieval evaluation uses the same suffix-style matching criterion that is central to DDR verification and dataset construction, which may favor DDR and makes the reported very large precision/recall gap difficult to interpret without human validation or an independent dependency benchmark.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the claimed open-source dataset link is blank in the manuscript, and key details such as exact Mathlib/Lean versions, extraction scripts, prompts, model checkpoints, baseline indexing configuration, and BEq/prover settings are not sufficiently specified.

The train/test setup is narrow: all evaluation is sampled from FineLeanCorpus, the same corpus used to construct DDR training data. There is no cross-dataset evaluation, deduplication analysis, or contamination check beyond splitting by sampled difficulty categories.

The downstream autoformalization improvements are positive but moderate, and the paper overstates some claims such as outperforming all baselines nearly everywhere; for example, strong ICL models remain better on Diff01 and competitive on several subsets.

The complexity claims are oversimplified. Suffix-array construction and lookup depend on total character length and output size, not merely the number of library objects N, and the paper does not provide enough implementation-level benchmarking to support online-service scalability claims.

Presentation quality needs work: several typos and formatting issues appear, figures/tables are hard to read in places, and some references or model names seem inconsistent. These issues do not invalidate the idea but reduce clarity and confidence.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and technically important bottleneck in Lean autoformalization: supplying library dependencies that reduce identifier hallucination and definitional mismatch.
The proposed generate-then-verify framing is simple and potentially useful, and the suffix-array check is a reasonable engineering device for validating candidate identifiers against a large library.
The experiments include both intrinsic dependency-retrieval metrics and downstream autoformalization metrics, which is the right evaluation structure for the stated contribution.
The paper reports consistent improvements of RA+DDR over RA and RA+R@k baselines on the FineLeanCorpus subsets, especially on harder dependency-heavy subsets.
weaknesses: The main empirical evidence is not sufficiently convincing for acceptance. The dependency labels appear to be extracted from formal code using the same suffix-style matching machinery later used for evaluation, which risks circularity: DDR is rewarded for reproducing surface identifiers rather than demonstrably retrieving semantically necessary dependencies.

The suffix-array contribution is overstated. It verifies string existence, not relevance or correctness, and the complexity discussion ignores important practical factors such as total concatenated string length, query length, output-size costs, ambiguity resolution, and false matches from suffix/name collisions.

Reproducibility is weak. The manuscript leaves the dataset URL blank, does not specify Lean/mathlib versions, does not provide enough prompt and pipeline detail in the main paper, and gives limited information about model checkpoints, filtering, data splits, and evaluation scripts.

The experimental design has serious leakage and fairness concerns. FineLeanCorpus is used to construct the DDR training data and also to evaluate, with only random 100-sample difficulty-based test subsets; there is no clear deduplication or source-level split to prevent near-duplicate or template leakage.

Baselines are not fully persuasive. DDR uses a strong Qwen3-32B generative retriever, while the retrieval baselines are fixed R@5/R@10 methods from prior work; the comparison does not isolate whether gains come from the proposed retrieval paradigm, model scale, training data, decoding, or evaluation matching.

Downstream gains are modest and uneven. RA+DDR improves over RA+R@k, but on several subsets it remains below or comparable to strong ICL systems such as Claude/GPT/Qwen, weakening the broader claim that the method is generally superior for autoformalization.

The paper relies heavily on BEq against FineLeanCorpus formal statements, but gives little independent validation that the predicted formalizations preserve the original informal meaning. This is especially concerning because some examples look underspecified or synthetic.

Claims about scalability, online deployment, and continuous improvement are not adequately substantiated by experiments beyond a processing-time anecdote. There is no ablation of verification method, library size, ambiguity rate, or latency under realistic service conditions.

Clarity and polish are below ACL standard: there are grammatical errors, malformed citations, missing citation text, compressed/poorly readable figures and tables, and some claims are repeated without precise definitions or evidence.

The open-sourced dataset is presented as a major contribution, but without a working link, schema details, license, construction script, quality audit, or manual validation, it cannot currently support a positive reproducibility judgment.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and important bottleneck in Lean autoformalization: supplying relevant Mathlib dependencies to reduce hallucinated identifiers and definitions. The problem is well motivated and highly relevant to NLP/formal reasoning.

The generation-plus-verification framing for Direct Dependency Retrieval is simple and practical. Using an LLM to propose dependencies, then validating them against the formal library, is a sensible alternative to fixed-top-k embedding retrieval.
The empirical gains in dependency retrieval are large: DDR substantially improves precision, recall, and F1 over the R@5/R@10 baselines across all difficulty groups.

The downstream autoformalization experiments are encouraging. RA+DDR improves over RA and RA+R@k on BEq across the tested subsets, and the multi-sample consistency/efficiency analyses support the claim that better dependencies improve stability, not only single-shot accuracy.

The work includes useful dataset construction at scale, with over 500k statement-dependency pairs, and the paper gives enough high-level methodological detail to understand how the labels are extracted and verified.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is weaker than it should be. The paper says the dataset is open-sourced, but the URL appears missing in the manuscript, and key implementation details for the suffix-array extraction, exact Mathlib version, prompts, filtering rules, and evaluation scripts are not sufficiently specified.

The comparison to retrieval baselines is limited. DDR is a fine-tuned 32B generative model, while the main retrieval baselines are fixed R@5/R@10 methods from prior work; stronger lexical/code-search baselines, modern dense retrievers, hybrid retrieval, or fine-tuned retrieval models would make the retrieval claim more convincing.

The dependency-retrieval evaluation relies on automatically extracted labels and suffix-based matching. This is practical, but it may reward surface identifier overlap and does not establish that the retrieved dependencies are semantically necessary or sufficient. Manual validation on a subset would strengthen the evidence.

There are possible data contamination and split concerns. FineLeanCorpus is used both to construct DDR training data and to sample evaluation sets, and although the authors split by held-out examples, duplicate or near-duplicate formalizations across difficulty levels or source datasets are not carefully ruled out.

Some claims are overstated. The suffix-array component is an efficient engineering device rather than a novel retrieval algorithm, and the stated O(log N) verification claim abstracts away query length, output size, delimiter handling, and ambiguity resolution.

The downstream gains, while consistent, are moderate compared with the very large gains in dependency retrieval. More analysis is needed to explain when high dependency precision/recall does or does not translate into correct autoformalization.

Presentation has several clarity and polish issues, including typos, malformed or missing citations/placeholders, unclear table formatting, and ambiguity about whether Table 3 reports @1 or @8 results.

strengths: Addresses an important and well-scoped problem for Lean autoformalization: retrieving Mathlib dependencies to reduce hallucination and improve formal statement generation.

The generation-plus-verification framing is practically useful. Using a library membership check to filter generated dependencies is a reasonable way to combine LLM flexibility with a hard validity constraint.
The paper evaluates both the intermediate retrieval task and downstream autoformalization, with multiple LLM baselines, SFT baselines, difficulty buckets, and TypeC/BEq metrics.
Results suggest DDR has much higher filtered dependency precision than select-based retrieval and prompt-only dependency generation, and downstream BEq generally improves for DeepSeek-R1 and RA.
The appendix includes useful implementation details such as prompts, decoding setup, model choice, and LoRA hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The empirical case is not yet strong enough for a clear Findings recommendation. The downstream gains are often small in absolute terms, sometimes absent or negative relative to no retrieval, and no confidence intervals, bootstrap tests, or significance analysis are provided for 200-example test subsets.

The comparison is potentially unfair: DDR is a 32B model fine-tuned on more than 500k in-domain examples, while many baselines are prompt-based retrieval methods or older/selective retrieval systems not given comparable supervised adaptation.

Reproducibility is weak. The paper claims an open-sourced dependency dataset but the URL is missing in the manuscript, and there is no code release, exact train/test split identifiers, exact Mathlib/Lean version, SAC implementation detail, or full BEq evaluation configuration sufficient to reproduce the numbers.

The retrieval evaluation may be inflated by the suffix/sublist matching criterion for short or ambiguous dependency names. The paper does not quantify ambiguity, false positives, or how often shortcut names map to multiple Mathlib objects.

The claimed novelty of SAC is limited: suffix arrays are standard, and the paper mainly applies exact/substring matching to library identifiers. The contribution is more engineering than algorithmic, but this distinction is not clearly acknowledged.

The dependency labels are extracted from existing formal code, which may be incomplete, stylistically variable, or not uniquely tied to the informal statement. The paper does not validate label quality with manual inspection or analyze missing/alternative valid dependencies.

The paper overstates conclusions about formalization difficulty. Depend Rate and Depend Length are plausible correlates but are not validated independently and may simply reflect properties of the labeling/extraction pipeline.

Several presentation issues reduce confidence: malformed text/tables, a missing dataset link, inconsistent notation, grammatical errors, and prompt examples that are not valid JSON despite requiring JSON output. These are not fatal, but they matter for a reproducibility-focused systems paper.

strengths: The paper addresses a real bottleneck in Lean autoformalization: generated formal statements often fail because models do not know or misuse Mathlib dependencies. The idea of separating dependency generation from downstream formalization is relevant to NLP-for-formal-math workflows.

The proposed DDR plus verification pipeline is simple and practically motivated. The reported dependency retrieval precision is substantially higher than the compared embedding-style R@k baselines, and the hallucination analysis is a useful diagnostic for generative dependency extraction.

The paper evaluates both retrieval quality and downstream autoformalization, using TypeC and BEq rather than only surface metrics. Testing DDR with both SFT-style and ICL autoformalizers is a reasonable attempt to show plug-in value.
A large dependency-labeled dataset, if actually released with sufficient metadata, could be useful for the community.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are overstated relative to the evidence. Downstream BEq improvements are often small, mixed, or absent: in Table 4 RA+DDR only marginally improves over RA+R@5/R@10, and in Table 5 DDR is not consistently better than no retrieval across models and difficulty splits. The text presents these as broad, significant gains without statistical testing or uncertainty estimates.

The evaluation design is fragile. Each difficulty bucket uses only 200 test examples, sampled from the same source corpus used to train DDR on all remaining examples. The paper does not convincingly rule out near-duplicate leakage, template overlap, or memorization of corpus-specific formalization conventions.

The dependency retrieval metric may not measure the claimed capability. Ground-truth dependencies are extracted from one formalization, but other valid formalizations may use different dependencies; conversely, extracted identifiers may be incidental rather than necessary. The suffix/sublist matching criterion is lenient and may inflate precision/recall through partial-name matches.

SAC is presented as a major methodological contribution, but it is mostly an existence check over strings. For dependency identifiers, the paper does not compare against simpler exact-match structures such as hash sets, tries, or prefix indexes, nor does it provide convincing runtime/memory benchmarks. The suffix-array choice is therefore under-justified.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The claimed open-access dataset link appears missing, the Lean/Mathlib versions are not specified, code is not provided, prompts contain malformed JSON examples, proprietary models are used without enough decoding/API details, and there are no seeds or variance estimates.

The baseline comparison is incomplete. DDR is a fine-tuned 32B model, but several baselines are prompt-only or older retrieval systems with different output formats. The paper lacks stronger supervised retrieval baselines, smaller-model ablations, and fair compute/model-size controls.

The difficulty analysis is speculative. Depend Rate and Depend Length may correlate with formalization difficulty, but the paper treats them as a potential sound difficulty measure without validating against human judgments or controlled task properties. The exclusion of Diff01 further weakens the generality of the claim.

Writing and presentation have many issues that reduce confidence: grammatical errors, formatting problems in tables and prompts, an empty dataset URL, unclear notation, and occasional incorrect or imprecise claims such as theorem provers being both sound and complete in a broad sense. These are not merely cosmetic because they obscure key experimental details.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely bottleneck in Lean autoformalization: models often fail because they do not know or correctly use Mathlib dependencies. The proposed DDR framing is well motivated and directly relevant to NLP-for-formal-math research.

The generation-plus-verification design is conceptually strong. Using SAC to validate generated dependency names gives the approach a practical guardrail against hallucinated library items, and the hallucination analysis is a useful contribution beyond the downstream task results.

The empirical retrieval results are compelling: DDR substantially improves filtered dependency precision and recall over both prompt-based dependency generation and prior select-based R@k retrieval baselines across difficulty splits.

The downstream experiments cover multiple autoformalization settings, including SFT-style RA baselines and several strong ICL models. The results generally show that DDR improves BEq/TypeC performance, especially for DeepSeek-R1 and RA+DDR.

The paper includes useful implementation details in the appendix, including prompts, decoding setup, BEq/TypeC definitions, DDR model choice, and fine-tuning hyperparameters, which helps reproducibility.
The construction of a large dependency-labeled dataset from FineLeanCorpus is potentially valuable for the community, and the difficulty-analysis angle is an interesting secondary contribution.
weaknesses: The reproducibility claim is weakened by an apparently missing open-access URL for the constructed dataset. Since the dataset is a central contribution, the paper should provide a working link, versioning information, exact Mathlib/Lean version, and code for SAC extraction and DDR inference.

The dependency labels are produced by string-level extraction and existence checking from formal code. SAC verifies that a candidate exists in the library, but not that it is semantically necessary or sufficient for autoformalization. This limits how strongly precision/recall over these labels can support claims about true dependency quality.

The downstream gains are positive but often modest, especially in BEq for RA+DDR over RA or R@5/R@10. The paper repeatedly describes the improvements as significant, but I do not see statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or variance across sampled test sets.

The experimental split samples only 200 examples per combined difficulty bucket from a much larger corpus. This gives clean controlled evaluation, but the paper should justify the sample size and report robustness to different random seeds or larger test subsets.

Fairness of retrieval comparisons is not fully settled. DDR is a fine-tuned 32B model trained on labels constructed from the same source corpus, while some baselines are prompt-based or prior retrievers with different output formats and available metadata. This makes the magnitude of the retrieval advantage harder to interpret.

The autoformalization setup may conflate dependency quality with prompt-format compatibility. The authors note that DDR outputs abbreviated names while RA expects richer metadata, but the paper does not fully explore whether expanding DDR outputs to full metadata would further improve results or whether the comparison penalizes some baselines.

The proposed difficulty metrics, Depend Rate and Depend Length, are plausible but preliminary. They are derived from the same dependency extraction process being evaluated, and the argument that they can assess formalization difficulty would benefit from stronger correlation analysis against model failures and human difficulty judgments.

Writing and presentation need polishing. There are grammatical errors, formatting artifacts in tables/figures, and some incomplete or awkward passages; these do not undermine the core idea, but they reduce clarity.
